marble.name: Erosion and weathering
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Make observations and measurements to provide evidence of the effects of weathering or the rate of erosion by water, ice, wind, or vegetation
marble.prompt: Can you look at a crumbling cliff or a river bank and explain how water, wind, or ice has slowly worn away the rock or soil over time?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning to observe and describe weather patterns and seasons, while exploring how plants and animals change their environment to meet their needs.

misconceptions: 'Weathering and erosion are the same' — conflating break-down with transport.
'Erosion is always fast/dramatic' — missing that much erosion is slow and gradual.
'Plants cause erosion' — not recognising vegetation usually PROTECTS soil (roots bind it), though roots can also weather rock.
'Harder rocks don't weather' — all rock weathers, just at different rates.
'A single trial proves it' — not valuing repeats/fair tests and measurement.
representations: A stream-table (sloped tray of soil/sand with controllable water flow).
A shake-jar abrasion test (rock chips shaken, measuring rounding/sediment produced).
A fair-test comparison table (variable changed → measured effect).
Before/after landscape photos or profiles showing change.
authoredAnswer: The child shakes the cubes and shows they break down and round in place (weathering), then shows the broken bits carried away by the water and settling elsewhere (erosion = movement, then deposition), and reads the riverbank photos as material worn away and moved over the year — keeping 'breaking in place' separate from 'being moved'.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Labels breaking-in-place as erosion, or transport as weathering; can't separate the two observations.
wrongAnswers.fix: Confront it — weathering breaks the rock where it sits, erosion carries the pieces away; demonstrate each step on its own.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Describes erosion but never says where the sediment ends up.
wrongAnswers.fix: Scaffold — 'where did the washed-off bits go?' and introduce deposition as the settling stage.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Only accepts sudden events as erosion; dismisses the small year-on-year change in the photos.
wrongAnswers.fix: Contrast rapid vs slow rates; use the photos to measure the small change over a year.
